setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A ventilated patient develops fever, purulent secretions and a new infiltrate on day 6. What sampling approach do the IDSA/ATS 2016 guidelines suggest?

options.B: Non-invasive sampling (endotracheal aspirate) with semiquantitative cultures
options.D: Mandatory bronchoscopic BAL with quantitative culture in all patients

explanation: IDSA/ATS suggest non-invasive sampling with semiquantitative cultures to diagnose VAP, because invasive quantitative methods have not improved outcomes. Cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when this does not delay therapy; blood cultures are also recommended.
referenceText: Kalil et al. 2016 (IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP) [109]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: When should empirical MRSA coverage be included for suspected VAP according to IDSA/ATS?

options.A: Only if Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods
options.B: Only in patients without prior antibiotic exposure
options.C: Never; MRSA coverage should await culture
options.D: In every patient with VAP, regardless of the local MRSA prevalence data or any prior antibiotic exposure
options.E: Resistance risk factors (e.g. IV antibiotics within 90 days) or unit MRSA prevalence >10–20% or unknown

explanation: IDSA/ATS recommend empirical MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) for VAP if there are risk factors for antimicrobial resistance, in units where more than 10–20% of S. aureus isolates are methicillin-resistant, or where prevalence is unknown. Antipseudomonal coverage is recommended for all empirical VAP regimens.
referenceText: Kalil et al. 2016 (IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP) [109]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: What antibiotic duration is recommended for most patients with VAP who respond clinically?
explanation: IDSA/ATS recommend 7 days of therapy for HAP and VAP, including non-fermenting Gram-negative organisms, with shorter or longer durations depending on clinical response. Radiographic resolution lags behind clinical improvement and should not determine duration.
referenceText: Kalil et al. 2016 (IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP) [109]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which oral care practice is recommended by the 2022 SHEA/IDSA/APIC compendium to reduce VAP?

options.D: No oral care to avoid aspiration
options.E: Chlorhexidine 2% oral rinse every 2 hours in all patients

explanation: The 2022 compendium recommends toothbrushing (associated with lower VAP and mortality) and states that chlorhexidine oral care is no longer recommended routinely because meta-analyses suggest possible increased mortality. Probiotics are not recommended.
referenceText: Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which group of measures is considered an essential practice for preventing VAP and ventilator-associated events?

options.B: Routine use of silver-coated endotracheal tubes and weekly circuit changes in all ventilated patients
options.D: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in all patients
options.E: Avoid intubation, minimise sedation, paired SAT/SBT, head-up positioning and early mobility

explanation: The compendium highlights avoiding intubation (NIV, HFNO), minimising sedation, paired SAT/SBT, early mobility, head-of-bed elevation (30–45°), and endotracheal tubes with subglottic drainage for patients expected to be ventilated more than 48–72 hours. Circuits should be changed only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning.
referenceText: Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which practice is part of the insertion bundle to prevent CLABSI?

options.C: Preferring the femoral site in obese adults
options.D: Maximal sterile barriers and chlorhexidine–alcohol skin antisepsis
options.E: Povidone-iodine without alcohol, with small drapes to limit contamination

explanation: Essential CLABSI practices include hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full-body drape), chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation, ultrasound guidance, avoiding the femoral site in obese adults, and daily review of line necessity. Prophylactic antibiotics and routine replacement are not recommended.
referenceText: Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: How does the differential time to positivity help diagnose catheter-related bloodstream infection?

options.A: Catheter-drawn culture growing ≥2 hours before a simultaneous peripheral culture suggests CRBSI
options.B: A single positive culture of coagulase-negative staphylococci from any site confirms the diagnosis of CRBSI
options.C: A catheter tip culture alone is sufficient
options.D: Growth from a peripheral culture first confirms CRBSI
options.E: Both cultures growing at the same time confirms CRBSI

explanation: When paired blood cultures are drawn simultaneously from the catheter and a peripheral vein, positivity of the catheter sample at least 2 hours earlier indicates a higher bacterial burden in the catheter, supporting CRBSI. Catheter tip cultures require catheter removal.
referenceText: Mermel et al. 2009 (IDSA catheter-related infection) [137]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient has S. aureus bacteraemia from an infected central line, which has been removed. What additional evaluation is essential?

options.D: Echocardiography (TOE if high risk) and repeat blood cultures to confirm clearance
options.E: No further evaluation is needed once the fever has resolved after removal of the line

explanation: S. aureus bacteraemia has a high risk of endocarditis and metastatic infection. Management includes source removal, repeat blood cultures, echocardiography, and at least 14 days of IV therapy for uncomplicated bacteraemia (4–6 weeks for complicated cases). Infectious diseases consultation reduces mortality.
referenceText: Mermel et al. 2009 (IDSA catheter-related infection) [137]; Delgado et al. 2023 (ESC infective endocarditis) [51]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient has methicillin-susceptible S. aureus bacteraemia and is receiving vancomycin empirically. What change is recommended?

options.A: Continue vancomycin, because it is equivalent to beta-lactams for MSSA bacteraemia
options.C: Switch to an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam (e.g. flucloxacillin, cefazolin)
options.D: Add rifampicin to vancomycin in all cases

explanation: For MSSA bacteraemia, beta-lactams (flucloxacillin, oxacillin, cefazolin) are associated with lower mortality than vancomycin. Routine gentamicin increases nephrotoxicity without benefit, and adjunctive rifampicin did not improve outcomes in the ARREST trial.
referenceText: Mermel et al. 2009 (IDSA catheter-related infection) [137]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A critically ill patient has Candida albicans candidaemia. What initial therapy do IDSA guidelines recommend?

options.A: No therapy if the patient is afebrile
options.C: Amphotericin B deoxycholate as first choice in all patients
options.D: An echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin, micafungin or anidulafungin)

explanation: IDSA recommends an echinocandin as initial therapy for candidaemia in most patients, especially the critically ill. Step-down to fluconazole is appropriate after 5–7 days if the isolate is susceptible and the patient is clinically stable with cleared cultures.
referenceText: Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which additional measures are recommended for a non-neutropenic patient with candidaemia?

options.A: Remove the CVC if feasible, dilated eye exam, and treat 14 days after first negative culture
options.B: Perform echocardiography only in neutropenic patients or those with a prosthetic heart valve
options.C: Treat for 6 weeks in all patients
options.D: No repeat blood cultures are required
options.E: Leave the catheter in place and treat for 3 days

explanation: IDSA recommends early CVC removal when the catheter is the presumed source, ophthalmological examination to detect endophthalmitis, daily or alternate-day blood cultures, and treatment for 2 weeks after documented clearance and symptom resolution in uncomplicated candidaemia.
referenceText: Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Why is Candida auris a major concern in ICUs?

options.A: It is uniformly susceptible to fluconazole
options.B: Often multidrug resistant, misidentified by standard methods and transmissible
options.D: It is reliably eradicated from the environment by alcohol hand rub and routine cleaning

explanation: C. auris causes outbreaks of invasive infection, persists on skin and surfaces, is frequently resistant to fluconazole and sometimes to other classes, and may be misidentified by conventional laboratory methods. Echinocandins are first-line; strict contact precautions and environmental cleaning with sporicidal agents are needed.
referenceText: Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient has symptomatic Candida albicans cystitis with a fluconazole-susceptible isolate. Why is an echinocandin a poor choice?

options.A: Echinocandins require dose adjustment in renal failure
options.C: Echinocandins have no activity against C. albicans
options.D: Echinocandins achieve very low urinary concentrations

explanation: Echinocandins are poorly excreted in urine. Fluconazole, which is renally excreted unchanged, is preferred for susceptible Candida urinary tract infections; amphotericin B deoxycholate or flucytosine are options for resistant species. Asymptomatic candiduria usually does not require treatment.
referenceText: Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which Candida species is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole?
explanation: C. krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole, and C. glabrata often has reduced susceptibility. C. parapsilosis has higher echinocandin MICs and is associated with catheters and parenteral nutrition. Species identification guides therapy.
referenceText: Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: An immunocompromised ventilated patient has nodular infiltrates with halo signs on CT and a positive BAL galactomannan. What is the recommended primary therapy?
explanation: IDSA recommends voriconazole as primary therapy for invasive aspergillosis, with isavuconazole or liposomal amphotericin B as alternatives. Therapeutic drug monitoring of voriconazole is recommended. Fluconazole has no activity against Aspergillus. Influenza-associated and COVID-associated aspergillosis occur in non-neutropenic ICU patients.
referenceText: Patterson et al. 2016 (IDSA aspergillosis) [164]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis develops facial swelling, black necrotic eschar on the palate and proptosis. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Broad-spectrum antibacterials alone for presumed bacterial orbital cellulitis
options.E: Liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent surgical debridement, correcting DKA

explanation: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis is associated with uncontrolled diabetes, ketoacidosis, steroids and iron overload. Treatment requires high-dose liposomal amphotericin B, aggressive surgical debridement and correction of the underlying condition. Voriconazole has no activity against Mucorales and may promote infection.
referenceText: Patterson et al. 2016 (IDSA aspergillosis) [164]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient develops diarrhoea with C. difficile toxin-positive stool, WBC 13 × 10⁹/L and creatinine normal. What is the preferred initial treatment according to IDSA/SHEA 2021?

options.A: Oral metronidazole as first choice in all patients
options.E: Oral fidaxomicin (oral vancomycin is an alternative)

explanation: The 2021 focused update suggests fidaxomicin over standard vancomycin for initial CDI, with oral vancomycin an acceptable alternative; metronidazole is only for non-severe cases when these are unavailable. IV vancomycin does not reach the colon. Antiperistaltics should be avoided.
referenceText: Johnson et al. 2021 (IDSA/SHEA C. difficile update) [104]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with C. difficile infection develops hypotension, ileus and megacolon. Which treatment regimen is recommended?

options.A: Oral fidaxomicin alone at standard dose, with loperamide for symptom control and IV fluids
options.C: Oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS plus IV metronidazole (rectal vancomycin if ileus), surgical review

explanation: Fulminant CDI (hypotension, shock, ileus or megacolon) is treated with high-dose enteral vancomycin, rectal vancomycin enemas when ileus is present, and IV metronidazole. Early surgical consultation (subtotal colectomy or loop ileostomy) is important for deteriorating patients.
referenceText: Johnson et al. 2021 (IDSA/SHEA C. difficile update) [104]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: What does the 2024 IDSA guidance suggest for treating carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection?

options.C: Sulbactam–durlobactam with a carbapenem, or high-dose ampicillin–sulbactam in combination
options.E: Ceftazidime–avibactam monotherapy at high dose, given as a prolonged 3-hour extended infusion

explanation: IDSA 2024 suggests sulbactam–durlobactam combined with meropenem or imipenem as preferred therapy; if unavailable, high-dose ampicillin–sulbactam in combination with another active agent (polymyxin B, minocycline, tigecycline or cefiderocol). Avibactam does not reliably inhibit Acinetobacter carbapenemases.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A ventilated patient has VAP due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to piperacillin–tazobactam, cefepime, carbapenems and fluoroquinolones. Which agent is preferred according to IDSA 2024?

options.A: Ceftolozane–tazobactam (or ceftazidime–avibactam or imipenem–relebactam per testing)
options.D: Aztreonam monotherapy at high dose, without waiting for any susceptibility test results

explanation: Difficult-to-treat resistant P. aeruginosa infections are preferentially treated with newer beta-lactams such as ceftolozane–tazobactam, ceftazidime–avibactam, imipenem–relebactam or cefiderocol, guided by susceptibility. Tigecycline and ertapenem lack reliable antipseudomonal activity.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: When colistin is used for a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection, which practice is recommended?

options.A: Use as monotherapy for bloodstream infections without other options considered
options.B: A loading dose followed by maintenance dosing, with monitoring for nephrotoxicity
options.C: Avoid in renal failure in all circumstances
options.D: Low doses without a loading dose to avoid toxicity

explanation: Colistin (polymyxin E) is administered as the prodrug colistimethate; a loading dose is required to achieve therapeutic concentrations rapidly. Dose-dependent nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity are common. Polymyxin B does not require renal dose adjustment and is preferred for systemic infections except UTI.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]; Abdul-Aziz et al. 2020 (antimicrobial TDM position paper) [1]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which antibiotic is a preferred option for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infection?
explanation: S. maltophilia is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems via a metallo-beta-lactamase. IDSA suggests combination therapy using two of co-trimoxazole, minocycline, tigecycline, levofloxacin or cefiderocol, or ceftazidime–avibactam plus aztreonam. Isolates from respiratory samples often represent colonisation.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient has bacteraemia with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. Which antibiotic is appropriate?

options.A: Vancomycin at higher dose by continuous infusion

explanation: VRE bacteraemia is treated with linezolid or high-dose daptomycin (8–12 mg/kg). Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, and E. faecium is usually resistant to ampicillin and carbapenems.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: For serious MRSA infections, what monitoring target do the 2020 consensus guidelines recommend for vancomycin?

options.A: Trough of 25–30 mg/L for all serious infections

explanation: The 2020 consensus recommends AUC-guided dosing (AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L) using Bayesian software or two levels, replacing trough targets of 15–20 mg/L, which were associated with more nephrotoxicity without better efficacy. A loading dose of 20–35 mg/kg can be considered in critically ill patients.
referenceText: Rybak et al. 2020 (vancomycin TDM consensus) [187]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient taking an SSRI is started on linezolid for MRSA pneumonia and develops agitation, hyperthermia, tremor and clonus. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Serotonin syndrome from linezolid's MAO inhibition
options.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from the SSRI

explanation: Linezolid is a weak non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor and can precipitate serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. Other adverse effects include thrombocytopenia and myelosuppression (especially beyond 2 weeks), lactic acidosis, and peripheral or optic neuropathy.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Boyer & Shannon 2005 (serotonin syndrome) [23]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Why is daptomycin not used to treat MRSA pneumonia?

options.A: It does not penetrate the bloodstream
options.B: It causes severe nephrotoxicity in the lungs
options.D: It has no activity against MRSA
options.E: It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant

explanation: Daptomycin binds to and is inactivated by surfactant, leading to treatment failure in pneumonia. It remains useful for MRSA bacteraemia and endocarditis. CK should be monitored because of myopathy, and statins may be paused.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Kalil et al. 2016 (IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP) [109]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which limitation of tigecycline is most relevant when treating bloodstream infections?

options.B: Marked nephrotoxicity requiring dose reduction in all patients with acute kidney injury
options.C: Low serum levels from a large distribution volume, plus an FDA mortality warning

explanation: Tigecycline distributes widely into tissues, resulting in low serum levels, making it unsuitable as monotherapy for bacteraemia. Meta-analyses showed increased mortality compared with other agents. It has no activity against Pseudomonas and is often used at high doses in combination for MDR infections.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with AKI receiving cefepime 2 g every 8 hours develops confusion, myoclonus and non-convulsive status epilepticus. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Uraemic encephalopathy alone from worsening AKI

explanation: Cefepime crosses the blood–brain barrier and antagonises GABA-A receptors; accumulation in renal impairment causes encephalopathy, myoclonus and non-convulsive seizures. Dose adjustment, therapeutic drug monitoring and EEG are important; dialysis accelerates removal.
referenceText: Abdul-Aziz et al. 2020 (antimicrobial TDM position paper) [1]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A long-term catheterised ICU patient develops fever without another source. How should urine be sampled for culture?

options.A: Replace the catheter (if in place >2 weeks) and sample from the new one
options.C: Collect urine after 7 days of antibiotics
options.D: Do not culture; start broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically for presumed urosepsis
options.E: Collect urine from the drainage bag

explanation: Long-standing catheters develop biofilms that do not reflect bladder urine. Replacing the catheter before sampling and treatment improves diagnostic accuracy and outcomes. Samples should never be taken from the drainage bag.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Mermel et al. 2009 (IDSA catheter-related infection) [137]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A catheterised ICU patient without fever or signs of infection has a urine culture growing E. coli 10⁵ CFU/mL. What is the appropriate management?

options.A: Treat with a 14-day course of meropenem for bacteriuria
options.D: No antibiotics; remove the catheter if no longer needed

explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients should not be treated, because treatment does not prevent symptomatic infection and promotes resistance and C. difficile infection. Exceptions include pregnancy and before urological procedures with mucosal bleeding.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A traveller returning from sub-Saharan Africa has Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia of 12%, impaired consciousness and AKI. What is the recommended treatment?

options.B: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then daily
options.D: IV quinine as first choice when artesunate is available

explanation: WHO recommends IV (or IM) artesunate for at least 24 hours for severe malaria, followed by a full course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy once oral intake is possible. Artesunate reduces mortality compared with quinine. Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis may occur.
referenceText: WHO Guidelines for malaria 2023 [241]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which feature defines severe falciparum malaria according to WHO?

options.C: Parasitaemia of 0.5% without any organ dysfunction, in a non-immune traveller
options.E: Impaired consciousness, convulsions, acidosis, AKI, shock or parasitaemia above 10%

explanation: WHO severe malaria criteria include impaired consciousness, prostration, multiple convulsions, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, renal impairment, jaundice, pulmonary oedema, significant bleeding, shock and hyperparasitaemia (above 10%). Any criterion mandates parenteral artesunate and high-dependency care.
referenceText: WHO Guidelines for malaria 2023 [241]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A farmer in rural Egypt presents with undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly and positive blood cultures for Brucella. What is a recommended first-line regimen for uncomplicated disease?

options.A: Ciprofloxacin monotherapy for 2 weeks, followed by oral amoxicillin for a further 4 weeks
options.B: Doxycycline for 6 weeks plus an initial aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin)

explanation: Brucellosis, endemic in Egypt and the Middle East, requires prolonged combination therapy to prevent relapse: doxycycline for 6 weeks with streptomycin (2–3 weeks) or gentamicin (7 days), or doxycycline plus rifampicin. Endocarditis, spondylitis and neurobrucellosis require longer, triple therapy.
referenceText: Ariza et al. 2007 (Ioannina brucellosis recommendations) [12]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A farmer with a neglected foot wound develops trismus, opisthotonus and generalised spasms. Which combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Tetanus immunoglobulin, metronidazole, debridement, benzodiazepines and airway protection
options.D: Low-dose penicillin alone, with tetanus toxoid vaccination and observation on a general ward

explanation: Tetanus management includes neutralising unbound toxin with human tetanus immunoglobulin, eliminating the organism with metronidazole and debridement, controlling spasms with benzodiazepines, magnesium or neuromuscular blockade, early airway protection (often tracheostomy), and active immunisation after recovery because disease does not confer immunity.
referenceText: Yen & Thwaites 2019 (tetanus) [244]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A ventilated patient with severe tetanus develops labile hypertension, tachycardia and sweating. Which drug is commonly used to control both spasms and autonomic instability?
explanation: Magnesium sulfate reduces spasms and catecholamine release and stabilises autonomic dysfunction in tetanus. Unopposed beta-blockade (e.g. propranolol) has been associated with sudden death and hypotension. Morphine and clonidine are other options; autonomic dysfunction is a major cause of death.
referenceText: Yen & Thwaites 2019 (tetanus) [244]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which practice is the single most effective measure for reducing healthcare-associated infection transmission?

options.B: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for all ICU patients
options.D: Hand hygiene with alcohol-based hand rub at the WHO "five moments"
options.E: Routine use of gloves without hand hygiene

explanation: Hand hygiene before patient contact, before aseptic tasks, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact and after contact with patient surroundings is the cornerstone of infection prevention. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; soap and water are needed for C. difficile spores.
referenceText: Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]; Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: What is the benefit of daily chlorhexidine bathing in ICU patients?

options.D: Eliminates the need for hand hygiene
options.E: Reduces C. difficile spores on skin

explanation: Daily chlorhexidine gluconate bathing reduces skin bioburden, decreasing CLABSI and acquisition of MRSA and VRE. It is recommended as an essential practice for ICU patients older than 2 months. It has limited activity against spores.
referenceText: Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient is colonised with carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which infection control measure is most appropriate?

options.B: No precautions, because colonisation is not the same as infection
options.C: Contact precautions with single-room isolation or cohorting
options.E: Routine daily rectal swabs of staff

explanation: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales spread by contact, so patients should be isolated or cohorted with dedicated equipment, contact precautions, environmental cleaning and active surveillance. Decolonisation with antibiotics is not recommended.
referenceText: Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient has new fever on day 8 of ICU stay with no clear infectious source. Which is a recognised non-infectious cause of fever?
explanation: Non-infectious causes of fever in ICU include drug fever, venous thromboembolism, pancreatitis, acalculous cholecystitis, transfusion reactions, adrenal insufficiency, withdrawal states, central fever after brain injury and malignancy. Drug fever may be accompanied by eosinophilia and rash and resolves after stopping the drug.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with a nasotracheal tube and nasogastric tube for 10 days develops fever and purulent nasal discharge. CT shows fluid levels in the maxillary sinuses. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Ignore because sinusitis does not cause fever
options.C: Insert another nasal tube on the opposite side to allow drainage of the infected maxillary sinus
options.E: Remove nasal tubes (use oral routes), consider sinus aspiration and targeted antibiotics

explanation: Nasal tubes obstruct sinus drainage and are associated with nosocomial sinusitis, which can cause fever and VAP. Management includes removing nasal tubes, sinus drainage or aspiration and antibiotics guided by culture.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with an external ventricular drain develops fever, reduced consciousness and CSF pleocytosis with low glucose. What empirical therapy is recommended?

options.C: Vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem)
options.D: Ceftriaxone alone at meningitic doses, plus dexamethasone and an oral antifungal

explanation: IDSA recommends vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam for healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis, covering staphylococci and resistant Gram-negative organisms. Infected drains should be removed; intraventricular antibiotics are considered when systemic therapy fails.
referenceText: Tunkel et al. 2017 (IDSA healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis) [218]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with prolonged neutropenia after chemotherapy remains febrile after 5 days of broad-spectrum antibacterials with no identified source. What should be considered?

options.B: Empirical or pre-emptive mould-active antifungal therapy, guided by CT chest and galactomannan
options.E: Granulocyte transfusion in all patients with persistent neutropenic fever

explanation: IDSA recommends empirical antifungal therapy and investigation for invasive fungal infection in high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever after 4–7 days of antibiotics. Chest CT and serum galactomannan support a pre-emptive approach. Fluconazole lacks mould activity.
referenceText: Freifeld et al. 2011 (IDSA febrile neutropenia) [71]; Patterson et al. 2016 (IDSA aspergillosis) [164]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A neutropenic patient after chemotherapy develops fever, right lower quadrant pain and diarrhoea. CT shows caecal wall thickening. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.C: Bowel rest, broad-spectrum Gram-negative and anaerobic cover, and surgical review
options.E: Immediate right hemicolectomy in all cases, before antibiotics or resuscitation are started

explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) is treated conservatively with bowel rest, IV fluids, antipseudomonal broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem) and G-CSF in some cases. Surgery is reserved for perforation, persistent bleeding or deterioration. Endoscopy risks perforation.
referenceText: Freifeld et al. 2011 (IDSA febrile neutropenia) [71]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which serious adverse effect is associated with fluoroquinolones?

options.A: Ototoxicity in all patients, especially when combined with loop diuretics
options.B: Aortic aneurysm or dissection, tendon rupture and QT prolongation

explanation: Regulatory warnings highlight fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, dysglycaemia and an increased risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection. They also promote C. difficile and can worsen myasthenia gravis.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient's blood culture is positive for Gram-positive cocci in clusters; a rapid PCR panel identifies S. aureus with no mecA gene within 2 hours. How should therapy be adjusted?

options.A: Stop all antibiotics because the PCR is negative for resistance
options.B: Wait for final susceptibility results in 72 hours before any change
options.D: Switch from empirical vancomycin to an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam

explanation: Rapid molecular diagnostics allow earlier optimisation: absence of mecA indicates MSSA, and beta-lactams are superior to vancomycin for MSSA. Integration of rapid diagnostics with stewardship programmes shortens time to optimal therapy. SSC 2026 recommends de-escalation once a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibilities are available (strong, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Why do hydrophilic antibiotics such as beta-lactams often require full or increased loading doses in septic shock, regardless of renal function?

options.A: Renal clearance is always reduced in sepsis
options.B: Absorption from the gut is enhanced
options.C: Hepatic metabolism of beta-lactams is induced by inflammation
options.D: Capillary leak and resuscitation increase volume of distribution

explanation: In sepsis, an expanded extracellular volume increases the distribution of hydrophilic drugs, lowering initial concentrations. Loading doses depend on volume of distribution, not clearance, so they should not be reduced for renal impairment; maintenance doses are adjusted for clearance.
referenceText: Abdul-Aziz et al. 2020 (antimicrobial TDM position paper) [1]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with uncomplicated E. coli bacteraemia from a urinary source becomes afebrile and stable within 48 hours of appropriate therapy. What treatment duration is supported by randomised evidence?
explanation: Yahav et al. showed that 7 days was non-inferior to 14 days for uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia in patients who were afebrile and stable by day 7. Shorter courses reduce antibiotic exposure and resistance. Uncontrolled sources and immunosuppression may require longer therapy.
referenceText: Yahav et al. 2019 (7 vs 14 days for Gram-negative bacteraemia) [243]; Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with a contaminated crush injury develops severe pain, tense swelling, crepitus and bronze skin discoloration within 24 hours, with Gram-positive rods in the wound exudate. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Oral amoxicillin, limb elevation and daily review on the surgical ward
options.E: Urgent surgical debridement with high-dose penicillin and clindamycin

explanation: Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene), usually caused by C. perfringens, progresses rapidly with toxin-mediated tissue necrosis and shock. Urgent radical debridement or amputation is essential, with penicillin and clindamycin (to suppress toxin production). Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct where available.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Which endotracheal tube feature is recommended for patients expected to require ventilation for more than 48–72 hours to reduce VAP?

options.A: A port for subglottic secretion drainage
options.B: A smaller diameter tube to reduce mucosal contact
options.E: A tube with a high-volume low-pressure cuff inflated to 50 cmH2O

explanation: Endotracheal tubes with subglottic secretion drainage reduce VAP by aspirating secretions pooled above the cuff. The compendium recommends them for patients likely to need ventilation beyond 48–72 hours. Cuff pressure should be kept at 20–30 cmH2O.
referenceText: Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: During a rapid infusion of vancomycin 1.5 g over 20 minutes, a patient develops flushing and pruritus of the face and upper body with mild hypotension. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Pause the infusion, give an antihistamine and restart more slowly (≤1 g/h)
options.C: Stop vancomycin permanently, because this reaction represents IgE-mediated anaphylaxis
options.D: Switch to teicoplanin because cross-reactivity is universal

explanation: Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly "red man syndrome") is caused by non-IgE histamine release related to infusion rate. It is managed by stopping the infusion, giving antihistamines and restarting more slowly; it is not a contraindication to future use. True anaphylaxis is rare.
referenceText: Rybak et al. 2020 (vancomycin TDM consensus) [187]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A transplant recipient has a fever and pulmonary nodules with halo sign on CT. What is likely?
explanation: Pulmonary nodules with a halo sign (ground-glass surrounding a nodule, representing haemorrhage around an angio-invasive fungal lesion) in an immunocompromised host suggest invasive aspergillosis; later an air-crescent sign may appear. Send serum and BAL galactomannan and fungal cultures. Voriconazole is first-line (isavuconazole is an alternative with fewer interactions, liposomal amphotericin B if azoles are contraindicated); remember that azoles raise tacrolimus levels. Mucormycosis (reversed halo sign) needs amphotericin. Pneumocystis causes diffuse ground-glass opacities, and CMV causes bilateral interstitial changes.

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A patient with neutropenic fever (ANC 0.3) is hypotensive. What is the first antibiotic?

options.C: Await blood cultures before choosing therapy
options.D: IV vancomycin alone, pending culture results

explanation: Febrile neutropenia with hypotension is septic shock in a high-risk patient. Give an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, cefepime or ceftazidime) within 60 minutes, after blood cultures, with fluids and vasopressors. In shock, guidelines add an aminoglycoside and vancomycin (or other Gram-positive cover) because of instability, and consider MDR cover based on local resistance. Delaying antibiotics for cultures increases mortality, vancomycin alone misses Gram-negatives such as Pseudomonas, and oral therapy is only for stable low-risk patients.

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: In neutropenic fever, when is vancomycin added?

options.B: Routinely in all patients with neutropenic fever
options.C: Instability, line or skin infection, or MRSA risk

explanation: Routine empirical vancomycin does not improve outcomes in febrile neutropenia and promotes resistance. IDSA/ESCMID guidance adds Gram-positive cover for haemodynamic instability, suspected catheter-related infection, skin or soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, known MRSA colonisation, or Gram-positive cocci in blood cultures before identification, and stops it after 48–72 hours if no resistant Gram-positive organism is found. Waiting 7 days or never adding it ignores these indications.

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A neutropenic patient has persistent fever after 5 days of antibiotics. What is the next step?

options.A: Switch to a carbapenem and repeat cultures only
options.B: Stop antibiotics and observe off treatment
options.C: Add an aminoglycoside and continue current therapy

explanation: Persistent fever after 4–7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics in a high-risk neutropenic patient raises concern for invasive fungal infection, mainly Aspergillus and Candida. Investigate with chest CT, serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan, and start empirical antifungal therapy (for example liposomal amphotericin B, caspofungin or voriconazole), or pre-emptive therapy guided by CT and biomarkers. Continue the antibacterials and look for occult sources. Adding an aminoglycoside without a new indication adds toxicity, and stopping antibiotics is unsafe while neutropenic.

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: Neutropenic patient has right lower quadrant pain, fever and bowel wall thickening. What is likely?
explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) is necrotising inflammation, usually of the caecum, after cytotoxic chemotherapy: fever, right lower quadrant pain and diarrhoea with neutropenia. CT shows bowel wall thickening above 4 mm, pneumatosis or perforation. Management is bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negatives and anaerobes (for example piperacillin-tazobactam), G-CSF and correction of coagulopathy; surgery is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or clinical deterioration. Appendicitis is less common and surgery carries high risk in neutropenia.

setTitle: Infections in the ICU and Antimicrobial Therapy
stem: A cancer patient on chemotherapy has neutropenia and fever. What is MASCC score used for?
explanation: The MASCC risk index identifies low-risk febrile neutropenia using burden of illness, absence of hypotension, absence of COPD, solid tumour or no previous fungal infection, no dehydration, outpatient onset and age under 60. A score of 21 or more (maximum 26) indicates low risk of serious complications, so selected patients may receive oral antibiotics or outpatient care. It is not a mortality score for ICU patients, does not diagnose sepsis and does not guide antifungal choice. CISNE is an alternative for solid tumours.
